text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementGeneticsSchizophrenia’s Cruel Roulette WheelGenetics and stress can combine in ways we don’t yet fully understandKFBy Kristen French11:00 AM CDT on September 1, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleWhen she was a young girl, Consuelo Walss-Bass’ mother Eugenia unraveled. Eugenia began hearing and speaking with disembodied voices, locking her children in the basement, chasing them with a belt, sometimes beating them violently. Eugenia grew up in Mexico, but moved with her husband Rodolfo to the United States shortly after they were married. She knew almost no one in some of the cities where the family lived, and her husband was often away tending to his OBGYN patients or out in the evenings with friends. The stress of raising her children in relative isolation became too much for Eugenia to bear. The children handled their mother’s illness the best that they could, trying to avoid her when she was in one of her moods. Subscribe to skip adsFeatured VideoThen a second tragedy struck. Consuelo’s youngest sister Paty—beautiful, gregarious and creative—began to fall apart when she was a teen. At first, she was just failing her classes, having trouble making friends, getting bullied by her peers, but then on a fateful family trip to Orlando, Paty had a mental break. She never fully recovered. Eventually, it became clear not only that Eugenia had schizophrenia but that Paty had it, too. The rest of the siblings were spared: Consuelo, Jenny, Leo and Rudy all went on to have successful careers and families. Read more: “The Faulty Weathermen of the Mind”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
